Worked with Bible societies and later Wycliffe/SIL on vernacular translation across West and East Africa.
SIM and AIM were prominent in post-war evangelical mission networks such as the IFMA and the Lausanne movement.

Joined Scottish and CMS missions in Kenya in the 1929 stand against female circumcision.
Shared the evangelical commitment to evangelising unreached peoples and to biblical authority.

disagreements.text: Rejected the theological liberalism they perceived in the International Missionary Council and later the WCC; most faith missions joined the separate Interdenominational Foreign Mission Association (1917) instead.
Opposed African independent and prophet churches over polygamy, healing practices and traditional rites; many independent churches in Kenya arose in reaction to mission policy in 1929–31.
Faith missions criticised denominational boards for institutionalism and comity agreements that, they argued, left the interior unevangelised.

deviations: Founded as lean pioneering movements, they became large institutional missions with hospitals, schools and radio stations.
The ideal of rapid evangelism and moving on gave way to decades of missionary control before transfer to African churches.
Initial resistance to higher education was reversed after the 1950s as African churches demanded it.

missions.name: Student Volunteer Movement for Foreign Missions
missions.statusNote: After peaking around 1920 the SVM declined amid theological liberalisation, post-war disillusion with missions, the Depression and the rise of conservative alternatives. It merged into the National Student Christian Federation in 1959, which became the University Christian Movement in 1966; the UCM dissolved itself in 1969. Its evangelical mission-mobilising role passed to InterVarsity's Urbana conventions and similar movements.
missions.summary: Born at D. L. Moody's student conference at Mount Hermon in 1886, the SVM recruited university students to pledge themselves to foreign missionary service under the watchword 'the evangelization of the world in this generation'. Led by John R. Mott, Robert Wilder and Robert Speer, it sent some 20,000 volunteers abroad by 1945, inspired parallel movements in Britain, Europe and Asia, and supplied leaders for Edinburgh 1910 and the ecumenical movement — before collapsing in the mid-20th century.
missions.story:
In July 1886 some 250 college students gathered for a month at Mount Hermon, Massachusetts, at the invitation of the evangelist Dwight L. Moody. Robert Wilder of Princeton, son of a former ABCFM missionary in India, had already formed a Princeton Foreign Missionary Society whose members signed a pledge to go abroad. At Mount Hermon he and others, encouraged by A. T. Pierson's preaching and by a 'meeting of ten nations' at which sons of missionaries and foreign students spoke, persuaded one hundred students to sign — the 'Mount Hermon Hundred'. In 1886–87 Wilder and John Forman toured 162 colleges and enrolled more than 2,000 volunteers. The movement was formally organised in 1888 as the Student Volunteer Movement for Foreign Missions, with John R. Mott as chairman, and linked to the YMCA, YWCA and the Inter-Seminary Missionary Alliance.

The SVM's watchword, 'the evangelization of the world in this generation', adopted in 1888 from Pierson, expressed its evangelical urgency and its practical optimism. As Mott explained in his book of that title (1900), it did not mean the conversion of the world but giving every person an adequate opportunity to hear the gospel within the lifetime of the present generation, by mobilising the church's resources efficiently. Volunteers signed a declaration: 'It is my purpose, if God permit, to become a foreign missionary.' The movement worked through campus 'bands', travelling secretaries, mission study classes and quadrennial conventions, beginning at Cleveland in 1891 and reaching a climax at Des Moines in 1919–20, which drew nearly 7,000 delegates.

The SVM became international. The Cambridge Seven's departure for China in 1885 and J. E. K. Studd's visit to America helped inspire it; in Britain the Student Volunteer Missionary Union was formed in 1892 and, through its Liverpool convention of 1896, adopted the watchword. In 1895 at Vadstena Castle in Sweden Mott and others founded the World's Student Christian Federation, and Mott's world tour of 1895–97 established student Christian movements in India, Ceylon, Australasia, China and Japan. Volunteers staffed the denominational boards and faith missions alike, and by 1945 about 20,000 had sailed — a large share of all American Protestant missionaries in that period, and a growing proportion of them women.

The SVM's leaders shaped the 20th-century missionary movement. Mott chaired the Edinburgh World Missionary Conference of 1910 and its Continuation Committee, then the International Missionary Council (1921), and received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1946; Robert Speer led the Presbyterian board for decades; J. H. Oldham, a British volunteer, organised Edinburgh 1910. The movement thus became a principal bridge between the evangelical revivalism of Moody and the ecumenical movement.

Its decline was swift. The First World War shattered confidence in 'Christian civilisation'. At Des Moines in 1920 students challenged the leadership about racism, imperialism and war, and by the Indianapolis convention of 1923–24 speakers such as Sherwood Eddy and Kirby Page turned the focus to social questions; the watchword was quietly abandoned. The fundamentalist–modernist controversy divided its constituency; the Laymen's Foreign Missions Inquiry (Re-Thinking Missions, 1932) questioned the very aim of conversion; and the Depression cut board budgets, so that volunteers who were enrolled could not be sent. Enrolments and sailings fell steeply after the early 1920s. Conservative students turned to new bodies — the Student Foreign Missions Fellowship (1936) and Inter-Varsity Christian Fellowship, whose missionary conventions began in Toronto in 1946 and moved to Urbana, Illinois, in 1948. In Britain the evangelical Cambridge Inter-Collegiate Christian Union had already disaffiliated from the Student Christian Movement in 1910, and the Inter-Varsity Fellowship (1928) carried forward its evangelical mission emphasis.

In 1959 the SVM merged with other student Christian bodies into the National Student Christian Federation, which became the University Christian Movement in 1966; amid the student radicalism of the late 1960s the UCM voted itself out of existence in 1969. The SVM's watchword and methods — student conventions, pledge cards and mobilisation — lived on chiefly among evangelicals, at Urbana and in later movements of short-term mission and unreached-peoples mobilisation.
beliefs: Evangelical conviction that all people need to hear the gospel of Christ and that Christians bear responsibility for making it known everywhere.
The watchword 'the evangelization of the world in this generation', understood as giving every person an adequate opportunity to hear the gospel within one lifetime.
A practical, activist and optimistic faith that well-organised, consecrated effort by Christian students could complete the task.
Commitment to Christian unity across denominations in the service of mission, which led many leaders into the ecumenical movement.
A holiness-influenced call to personal consecration and surrender, inherited from Moody, Keswick and Northfield.
From the 1910s, an increasingly social and liberal emphasis on the 'kingdom of God', character and the Christianisation of social order, which displaced the earlier evangelistic urgency.
strategies: The volunteer declaration card, signed by students pledging to become foreign missionaries 'if God permit'.
Travelling secretaries who visited campuses to recruit, form mission study bands and connect volunteers to sending boards.
Quadrennial conventions (Cleveland 1891 to Des Moines 1919–20 and beyond) that drew thousands of students.
Mission study textbooks and courses, producing an informed, mission-supporting laity.
Partnership with denominational boards, which did the actual sending, rather than sending missionaries itself.
Internationalisation through the World's Student Christian Federation (1895) and Mott's world tours.
groupsReached: American and Canadian college and seminary students, especially from evangelical Protestant denominations.
Women students, who became a majority of volunteers in some periods and filled women's mission boards.
British, Scandinavian, German and other European students through the SVMU and WSCF.
Students in India, China, Japan and Ceylon through student Christian movements founded on Mott's tours.
Indirectly, the peoples of Asia, Africa, Latin America and the Middle East served by some 20,000 volunteers.
challenges: Translating a pledge into actual service: many volunteers never sailed for reasons of health, family or board finances.
Theological polarisation between conservative and liberal students during the fundamentalist–modernist controversy.
Disillusionment after the First World War with Western 'Christian civilisation' and with missions' ties to empire.
Criticism from students of colour and international students about racism within the churches and the movement.
The Great Depression, which forced boards to cut missionary appointments drastically.
harms: Its 'crusading' language and assumptions of Anglo-Saxon Protestant superiority reinforced cultural imperialism, as later SVM leaders themselves admitted.
Optimistic rhetoric about 'evangelizing the world in this generation' sometimes encouraged superficial, numbers-driven approaches to mission.
The movement was slow to address segregation and racism in American churches and campuses until challenged in 1920.
Its later liberal drift alienated much of its evangelical base, contributing to a lasting split between ecumenical and evangelical student movements.
developments: Mobilised roughly 20,000 missionaries between 1886 and 1945, a major source of personnel for Protestant missions.
Created the World's Student Christian Federation (1895), a cradle of the ecumenical movement.
Supplied the leadership of Edinburgh 1910, the International Missionary Council and later the World Council of Churches.
Pioneered mission study education and mass student conventions, a model later used by Urbana and other mobilisation movements.
Encouraged indigenous student Christian movements in Asia that produced national church leaders.
missions.outcome: The SVM was the largest student mission mobilisation in history up to its time and the training ground of the ecumenical movement's leaders, but lost its evangelistic watchword after 1920, shrank in the 1920s–30s and dissolved through mergers by 1969, leaving its mobilising role to evangelical successors such as Urbana.

journeys.people: John R. Mott (with Leila White Mott for part of the tour)
journeys.text: After founding the World's Student Christian Federation at Vadstena in August 1895, Mott travelled through Europe and the Middle East to India, Ceylon, Australasia, China and Japan, organising national student Christian movements.

relations.text: SVM and WSCF leaders (Mott, Oldham, Speer, later W. A. Visser 't Hooft) organised Edinburgh 1910 and led the International Missionary Council and the WCC.
InterVarsity's Urbana conventions (from 1946/48) and later youth mission movements inherited the SVM's model of student mission mobilisation.
Many volunteers joined the CIM and other faith missions, and the Cambridge Seven helped spark the movement.

agreements.text: Shared commitment to interdenominational cooperation, comity and the unity of the church in mission.
In its first decades shared the urgent, premillennially tinged evangelism and consecration spirituality of the faith missions.

disagreements.text: Evangelical student movements such as InterVarsity and the Student Foreign Missions Fellowship arose partly in reaction to the SVM's liberal turn and loss of evangelistic focus.
By the 1920s faith missions distrusted the SVM's social-gospel orientation and increasingly recruited through Bible institutes rather than SVM bands.

deviations: Abandoned its founding watchword in the 1920s, moving from evangelistic urgency to social and international concerns.
A movement founded at a revivalist conference drifted toward the theological liberalism its founders would not have recognised.
From recruiting missionaries it became largely a forum for student debate on race, war and economics before dissolving.
